title: Academic Laboratories and the Reproduction of Proprietary Science: Modeling Organizational Rules through Autocatalytic Networks
pub: Chapter 16 in John F. Padgett & Walter W. Powell (eds.), The Emergence of Organizations and Markets, Princeton University Press, 2012, pp. 496–519
author: Jeannette A. Colyvas · Spiro Maroulis

dom.t: Innovation networks: Open anchors can sustain elites

st.t: Innovation networks: Open anchors can sustain elites
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s relational and institutional account and materially develops it by specifying how existing scientific practices are recombined across boundaries, while flexible university rules enable a self-reproducing public–proprietary regime. Its Stanford-focused counterfactual also reinforces the cluster’s caution against treating this mechanism as universal.
qs: Our approach to this question examines how disparate elements of the social organization of academic science- were assembled, transposed, and recombined to define a new regime of public and proprietary knowledge production.

A university of a different character, for example, one that was much more rigid and imposing in the application of norms and poli- cies, would have made laboratory-level assembly and flow of practices difficult.

st.t: Regional innovation: Network sequence matters more than volume
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s network-based account of novelty and materially extends it by identifying institutional flexibility—mutable categories, norms and policies—as a mechanism enabling practices to circulate through laboratory affiliation networks. Its caution about differing starting points also reinforces the cluster’s process-contingent, non-recipe framing, though it does not directly test the claim that local-to-distant network sequence matters more than connection volume.

kp.k: Institutional transformation can emerge from efforts to preserve autonomy
kp.d: Colyvas and Maroulis examine academic life science, not AI or legal services. Their central argument is that scientists' attempts to preserve academic autonomy and extend research programs helped transform open science into a hybrid public–proprietary regime. New practices were selectively assembled within existing scientific routines rather than simply imported wholesale from commerce.
qs: Consequently, our analysis shows that efforts to operate within the social structure of science generated the mecha- nism that transformed it.
When transposition happens, new practices are assem- bled selectively rather than adopted wholesale

kp.k: Archival evidence grounds counterfactual computational analysis
kp.d: The study combines archival analysis of one Stanford biomedical department between 1968 and 1982 with NetLogo agent-based modeling. Administrative records, invention files and correspondence support analysis of forty-one inventions linked to originating laboratories. Simulations operationalize proposed mechanisms and examine counterfactual combinations that historical records cannot independently resolve.
qs: We focus on a single biomedical de- partment at Stanford University, between 1968 and 1982
A sample of forty-one inventions from the basic life science department was identified and linked to a laboratory of ori- gin.
providing a platform to explore counterfactual scenarios that are impossible to investigate with histori- cal records.

kp.k: Laboratory practices preceded coherent policy implementation
kp.d: The archives suggest that commercialization approaches originated more in laboratories than in government, legal or university directives. Stanford's OTL began as a pilot program in 1968; participation was voluntary unless a funder required patenting. Ambiguous reporting requirements and reliance on scientists' industry relationships permitted substantial discretion over what counted as an invention, who qualified as an inventor and how rewards were distributed.
qs: First, despite all the attention given to na- tional and local policies, approaches toward commercializing research emanated more from individual labs than government, legal, or uni- versity sources.
Scientists often opted not to report findings at all, simply stating that the particular research output was not an “invention” or even inappro- priate to patent.

kp.k: Patenting depended on research characteristics and professional identities
kp.d: Four laboratory approaches—Team Effort, Clear Boundaries, Non-Faculty Career and Fair Share—attached different meanings to patents. Patenting could attract industrial development expertise, be restricted to applications rather than basic science, support an industry career, or protect university discoveries from exploitation. Acceptance therefore depended on particular findings and professional purposes, not merely a general willingness to commercialize.
qs: For most scientists, the debate hinged on how basic or exclusively fundamental to science a particular finding was.
In contrast, some scientists viewed patenting as a means of pre- serving the ability to disseminate one’s science when threatened by others patenting similar or related work.

kp.k: Research control outweighed personal profit in early commercialization
kp.d: The authors argue that early patenting principally served research continuity, authority and expansion rather than personal enrichment. University policy entitled scientists to one-third of licensing revenues, but three of four laboratory directors refused personal revenues. By 1982, two laboratories would garner roughly $2.3 and $1.8 million respectively; nevertheless, six of ten departmental faculty did not disclose inventions during the early period. These observations qualify an explanation based solely on financial incentives.
qs: According to university policy, scientists were entitled to one-third of the revenues from inventions that were licensed to firms.
Yet three of the four lab directors refused personal revenues
Initially research funding for one’s lab was a much more salient concern than the prospect of per- sonal profit.

kp.k: Junior scientists' mobility challenged established laboratory authority
kp.d: Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers helped change commercialization practices as they developed careers and asserted claims to research and rewards. In 1981, a departing Lab I postdoc claimed her inventor shares contrary to the principal investigator's laboratory-wide policy. University support weakened the PI's authority; he subsequently listed himself as an inventor, making formal inventorship a means of asserting scientific credit and control.
qs: In 1981 a postdoc in Lab I who was leaving the university elected to take her inventor shares, defying the terms that the lab PI had set for everyone in his research program.
Being formally listed as an inventor became a means of asserting credit and control over the science, a claim that had previously been asserted solely by publication.

kp.k: Standardization recombined rather than preserved initial laboratory approaches
kp.d: The authors report that none of the initial laboratory approaches survived unchanged. By 1982, practices converged toward patenting basic research and accepting individual licensing rewards. New research tools, disputes over revenue distribution and junior scientists' participation altered earlier boundaries and helped shape university-wide policy, even though participants retained differing scientific agendas.
qs: As technology transfer expanded, no one laboratory approach survived in its original form.
Patenting basic research findings became the norm and the practice of donating revenues disappeared, as taking individual monetary re- wards from successful licenses became common.
The same practice of patenting facilitated different agendas of advance and reputation.

kp.k: Knowledge production and disclosure routines coevolve
kp.d: The model treats laboratories as repertoires of skills that transform scientific products, with disclosure routines governing whether findings are patented. Products have a basic-science importance score and labs have patentability thresholds, both from 1 to 100. Successful exchanges reproduce skills; unsuccessful laboratories disappear and are replaced by offspring of successful labs. Collegial networks and complementary production skills evolve together, representing self-reinforcing scientific production rather than independent adoption decisions.
qs: The basic idea of the model is that scientific labs use rou- tines to transform knowledge.
organizational routines in a field—the patenting practices in scientific labs—did not evolve independently from the actual work of the field—the production of knowledge.
Labs with no advancement routines left will die.

kp.k: Three mechanisms distinguish reproduction, learning and defensive anticipation
kp.d: Population-level reproduction transmits successful labs' patentability thresholds with random variation. Participatory adaptation moves a lab's threshold toward a transaction partner that received greater rewards. Preemptive adaptation instead raises the threshold just enough to patent a finding when a network neighbor would patent it, modeling concern about losing control. The authors observe all three in the historical setting but isolate them computationally.
qs: The model contains three distinct mechanisms for change: reproduction, participatory adap- tation, and preemptive adaptation.

if a lab has a network neighbor whose disclosure routine would lead to the patenting of the product, the lab will adjust its patentability threshold to the minimum level that allows it to patent the product itself.
In the real world, as captured in our archival analysis, one can observe all three mechanisms simultaneously taking place.

kp.k: Preemptive adaptation most readily generates widespread patenting
kp.d: The computational comparison repeats each experimental condition fifty times, comparing reproduction alone with reproduction plus either participatory or preemptive adaptation. Starting from a mean patentability threshold of fifteen, reproduction alone produces a mean of approximately thirty-eight, partly because mutation cannot push thresholds below zero. Participatory adaptation restrains increases by reinforcing initially low thresholds. Preemptive adaptation produces a much larger shift because small differences between neighboring labs can trigger successive defensive changes without a highly patent-oriented exemplar.
qs: We therefore repeated each run fifty times under each experimental condition.
Under the baseline case of “reproduction only” the mean threshold across labs shifted only to approxi- mately thirty-eight.
the preemptive adap- tation mechanism only needs small variation in thresholds nearby to prompt change
the participatory adaptation mechanism is actually re- inforcing the extant norm of low patentability thresholds already in place.

kp.k: Reward conditions qualify the comparative mechanism findings
kp.d: Preemptive adaptation is not the model's only route to widespread patenting. When patent-related skill rewards are replicated ten times instead of two, with non-patenting rewards unchanged, all tested mechanism conditions produce the target shift. Conversely, rewarding non-patenting skills tenfold still does not stop a large preemptive shift. Changing the weight assigned to partners in participatory adaptation also leaves the basic comparative result intact. These are simulation findings under specified reward rules, not measured historical effect sizes.
qs: Preemptive adaptation, however, is not the only way to achieve our outcome of interest in our simulation process.
This change was implemented by having the skills rewarded for being involved in successful transactions as a result of patenting replicated ten times instead of only two as in the baseline case
In this scenario, all adaptation mechanisms appeared to produce our outcome of interest.
Changing the weight put on this mechanism does not seem to change the basic story.

kp.k: Emergence differs from diffusion and subsequent institutional reinforcement
kp.d: The authors distinguish mechanisms capable of generating a new regime from those that spread or reinforce an established practice. Both participatory and preemptive adaptation are consistent with the reported association between patenting and patenting colleagues, but their modeled implications differ. Simulations establish the possibility of bottom-up emergence without centralized incentives, not definitive proof that a single mechanism historically caused Stanford's transition. The authors caution that other universities or fields may have different initial conditions and outcomes.
qs: the mechanisms that give rise to an institution can be quite different from those that reinforce it
it was possible that bottom-up processes alone could give rise to the system we observed
Other universities or fields may have exhibited different starting points and emergent distributions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Colyvas and Maroulis explain the emergence of proprietary academic science through bottom-up changes in laboratory practices, rather than making claims about AI or legal services.
pts.d: The authors argue that scientists' attempts to preserve research autonomy, secure credit, and extend research programs helped transform academic disclosure practices. Initially divergent approaches to invention, inventorship, revenues, and relations with industry were selectively recombined into more standardized patenting practices. Their computational model indicates that anticipation of colleagues' patenting—preemptive adaptation—can generate a substantial shift toward patenting even from an initial population reluctant to patent. Learning from more successful transaction partners—participatory adaptation—can instead reinforce the existing low-patenting norm. These are historical interpretations and model-based mechanism claims in academic science, not predictions about AI adoption.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines Stanford archival research with agent-based computational experiments comparing mechanisms under alternative reward structures.
pts.d: The archival component examines Office of Technology Licensing administrative records and invention files, including correspondence, and links 41 inventions in one basic life science department to their originating laboratories. The authors compare four laboratory approaches and their subsequent changes. Evidence against a simple personal-profit explanation includes principal investigators foregoing substantial inventor shares and six of ten departmental faculty not disclosing inventions during the early period. The NetLogo model compares reproduction alone, reproduction with participatory adaptation, and reproduction with preemptive adaptation, with 50 runs per experimental condition. Under the baseline reward structure, reproduction alone raises the mean patentability threshold from 15 to approximately 38; participatory adaptation restrains the increase, while preemptive adaptation produces a much larger shift. Strongly favoring patent rewards permits all tested mechanism combinations to produce a large shift; favoring publication rewards does not eliminate the preemptive effect. These simulations demonstrate possible mechanisms under specified assumptions, rather than independently identifying their historical causal magnitude.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The historical claims concern Stanford's early commercialization period, 1968–1982, and subsequent institutionalization; the model supplies conditional explanations, not calendar-dated forecasts.
pts.d: The archival study focuses on one Stanford biomedical department between 1968 and 1982. The authors describe convergence in practices by 1982 and fuller integration of commercialization by the 1990s. Their baseline simulation begins with low patentability thresholds and allows laboratory reproduction and selected adaptation mechanisms. Preemptive adaptation depends on a socially connected lab being willing to patent a finding that the focal lab would otherwise leave unpatented. Participatory adaptation depends on encountering a more highly rewarded transaction partner and can therefore reproduce existing norms. The authors qualify generalization by noting Stanford's institutional flexibility: more rigid university policies could impede local recombination, and other universities or scientific fields could have different initial and emergent distributions. No future implementation horizon is given.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected actors are academic laboratories, principal investigators, junior scientists, university administrators, and firms that develop or use academic discoveries.
pts.d: Laboratories alter what they consider patentable and how they pursue control, credit, resources, and research continuity. Principal investigators' authority over inventor designation and revenue allocation becomes subject to competing claims from collaborators and university policies. Graduate students and postdocs gain opportunities to assert inventorship and personal rewards, while their movement into new laboratories helps reproduce and modify practices. University technology-transfer arrangements develop through these local disputes and experiments. Firms become partners in extending research programs but also potential appropriators against whom scientists seek patent protection. At the domain level, the authors describe movement toward a hybrid public–proprietary disclosure regime. They do not establish consequences for legal employment, legal-service pricing, or access to justice.
